[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: true and false are yes/no answers that, as in C, spreadsheets or maths logic, can be written as 1 and 0 and added or multiplied. Java rule: boolean is a separate primitive type with only the two values true and false; they are not numbers, cannot take part in arithmetic and cannot be cast to or from int.
[1] misconception (M) -> BooleanIsNumber: wrong rule: true and false are the numbers 1 and 0, so a boolean can be used in arithmetic. Right rule: The boolean type has only the values true and false; they are not numbers in Java, so true + 1 and (int) true do not compile.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> BooleanIsNumber: Points to LT (boolean operators are evaluated from their truth tables, left operand first). Applied unevenly: the student uses the truth table for && in one row of a trace but an everyday reading (e.g. exclusive 'or', or 1/0 arithmetic) in another. (here mixing in: "true and false are the numbers 1 and 0, so a boolean can be used in arithmetic")
[3] misconception (M) -> ArithmeticInsteadOfBoolean: wrong rule: A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true). Right rule: A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false, e.g. boolean isLeapYear = (year % 4 == 0);.

[0] names_the_element (N): boolean is a primitive data type whose only values are the literals true and false.
[1] states_the_rule (S): The boolean type has exactly two values, true and false; its operations are && (and), || (or) and ! (not); comparisons produce booleans; only boolean expressions can control if, while and for; no cast converts between boolean and a numeric type.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): A boolean variable's value is fetched when the expression that contains it is evaluated; !, && and || then combine those values by their truth tables, left operand first, skipping the right operand of && or || when the left already decides the result.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The value is true or false, and println prints the words true or false; e.g. LeapYear prints true for 2004 and false for 1900.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): An assignment replaces the variable's value with true or false; a = !a flips it, so three flips starting from true leave false.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): int and boolean never convert into each other; an int becomes a boolean only through a comparison (year % 4 == 0), and an int condition such as if (n) does not compile.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A double reaches the boolean world only through a comparison such as (x < 3.1), which yields a boolean; there is no cast between double and boolean.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): char is a numeric (integral) type whose values can be compared ('a' < 'b' is a boolean), whereas boolean is not numeric; neither converts to the other.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): &&, || and ! accept only boolean operands and return a boolean; applying them to ints (if (x && y) with int x, y) is a compile-time error.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): Comparisons are the main producers of boolean values: they take two numbers and return true or false, which can then be stored in a boolean variable.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): boolean is one of the eight primitive types and the only non-numeric one.
[6] purpose_of_the_whole (P): A boolean variable plays the flag role: it records whether a condition holds (isLeapYear) or, as a one-way flag (Sajaniemi), whether something has happened yet, e.g. found = true inside a search loop and never reset.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> BooleanIsNumber: Applying ! twice restores the value (negation is its own inverse), so an even number of a = !a statements leaves a unchanged and an odd number flips it; changing a one-way flag's initial value from false to true breaks the search it records.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use boolean to hold a yes/no fact or a flag that later code tests; do not use it for counts or for more than two states (use int), and do not encode it as 0/1 ints.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Conditions and boolean variables require boolean values; numbers are not booleans. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: An int used as a condition (if (n), while (count)), an int assignment inside a condition (if (x = 5)), arithmetic on booleans (flag + 1) or a cast (int) flag.
wrong: A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true). | right: A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false.
wrong: true and false are the numbers 1 and 0, so a boolean can be used in arithmetic. | right: The boolean data type has only two possible values: true and false, and they are not numbers in Java.
wrong: A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true). | right: A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false.
A boolean holds true or false; a char holds a single character such as 'c'.
A double holds a number with a fractional part; a boolean holds only true or false.
An int holds an integer and is a numeric type for computing with numbers; a boolean holds only true or false and is used for computing with logical values.
A comparison such as a < b takes two numbers and produces a boolean result.
&&, || and ! are the operations defined on the boolean type: they take booleans and give a boolean.
boolean is one of the eight primitive types, the one used for true-false values.
